Dates and times as people write them, rather than as a machine counts them.

`Clock` gives `unix_millis` and `monotonic_millis` and that is the whole of
time in `std` until this module. An instant is enough to measure something
and not enough to say when it happened: reconciliation is bucketed by value
date and settlement date, a report covers a month, and a log line is read by
somebody who wants to know what day it was. None of that is expressible in
milliseconds since 1970.

## What is here and what is deliberately not

The **types** are here — a civil date, a time of day, the two together, and
a fixed offset from UTC — because they are vocabulary. Two libraries that
disagree about what a date is cannot exchange one, and
`docs/design/ecosystem.md` reserves exactly that case for `std`.

The **time zone database is not**, and cannot be. It is a dataset: Egypt
changes its rules, IANA cuts a release, and every binary already shipped is
wrong about the future. Nothing behind this document's compatibility promise
can be updated four times a year. So `std` owns `Offset` — the answer — and
a package or the host owns the rules that produce one.

That is not a limitation dressed up. A program that stores UTC and renders
with an offset it was handed is correct forever; a program that bakes in
zone rules is wrong the next time a government moves a clock.

## The proleptic Gregorian calendar, everywhere

One calendar, extended backwards past its adoption, which is what ISO 8601
and every database mean by a date. Years before 1 are negative and year zero
exists — again ISO's convention, and the one that makes arithmetic work
without a special case nobody remembers.

## Types

### Date

```khora
pub type Date = {
  year: Int,
  month: Int,
  day: Int,
};
```

A date on the proleptic Gregorian calendar.

`month` is 1 to 12 and `day` is 1 to the length of that month. Construct
through `Date::of`, which checks; the fields are public because a date is
its three numbers and hiding them would only mean writing three accessors.

### Time

```khora
pub type Time = {
  hour: Int,
  minute: Int,
  second: Int,
  milli: Int,
};
```

A time of day, to the millisecond.

**No leap seconds.** `second` is 0 to 59, and a minute is sixty seconds
here as it is in every database and every wire format worth naming. A
calendar that admitted 23:59:60 would push that into every comparison and
every subtraction to be correct about something almost nothing observes.

### DateTime

```khora
pub type DateTime = {
  date: Date,
  time: Time,
};
```

A date and a time, with no zone attached.

**Not an instant.** "The fourteenth at nine in the morning" is a different
kind of thing from "one and a half billion seconds after 1970": one names a
position on a calendar and the other names a moment, and turning either
into the other needs an offset. Keeping them apart is what stops a program
silently treating local wall time as UTC — the mistake that puts a
midnight-boundary report a day out twice a year.

### Offset

```khora
pub type Offset = {
  minutes: Int,
};
```

Minutes east of UTC.

`Offset::utc()` is zero, India is `+330`, and `-300` is New York in winter.
**A fixed number, not a zone**: a zone is a rule that says which offset
applies on a given date, and that rule is a dataset this module refuses to
carry. A caller gets one of these from a package or from the host and hands
it here.

## Methods

### Date

```khora
impl Date
```

#### of

```khora
pub fn of(year: Int, month: Int, day: Int) -> Option<Date>
```

A date, or `None` if there is no such day.

The thirty-first of February is refused rather than rolled forward into
March. Rolling is a policy — some systems clamp, some wrap, some raise —
and a library that picked silently would be picking for a caller who
nearly always has bad input rather than an interesting question.

#### to_days

```khora
pub fn to_days(self) -> Int
```

Days since the first of January 1970, which may be negative.

Howard Hinnant's `days_from_civil`, which is the algorithm every modern
date library uses: it is exact for the whole range of an `Int`, it needs
no table, and its shifts of the year and month are what remove the leap
day from the middle of the calculation by moving March to the start of
the year.

#### of_days

```khora
pub fn of_days(days: Int) -> Date
```

The date `days` after the first of January 1970.

The inverse of `to_days`, and the other half of Hinnant's pair.

#### add_days

```khora
pub fn add_days(self, days: Int) -> Date
```

The date `days` later, which may be earlier if `days` is negative.

#### days_until

```khora
pub fn days_until(self, other: Date) -> Int
```

How many days from `self` to `other`, negative if `other` is earlier.

#### weekday

```khora
pub fn weekday(self) -> Int
```

Monday is 1 and Sunday is 7, which is ISO 8601's numbering.

The first of January 1970 was a Thursday, which is where the 3 comes
from: it is day zero and Thursday is 4, so the offset that lands Monday
on 1 is three.

### DateTime

```khora
impl DateTime
```

#### of_unix_millis

```khora
pub fn of_unix_millis(millis: Int) -> DateTime
```

The moment `millis` after 1970, as UTC says it.

**Flooring, not truncating**, which is the whole of what makes dates
before 1970 come out right: `-1` millisecond is the last millisecond of
1969, not the first of 1970 with a minus sign. Truncating division puts
it a whole day out, and it is the bug this function exists to not have.

#### to_unix_millis

```khora
pub fn to_unix_millis(self) -> Int
```

Milliseconds since 1970, reading `self` as UTC.

#### at_offset

```khora
pub fn at_offset(millis: Int, offset: Offset) -> DateTime
```

The same moment, seen from `offset`.

The one place a zone enters, and it enters as a number somebody else
worked out.

#### from_offset

```khora
pub fn from_offset(self, offset: Offset) -> Int
```

Milliseconds since 1970, reading `self` as a wall clock at `offset`.

## Functions

### days_in_month

```khora
pub fn days_in_month(year: Int, month: Int) -> Int
```

Days in `month` of `year`, which is only interesting for February.

### is_leap

```khora
pub fn is_leap(year: Int) -> Bool
```

Whether `year` has a twenty-ninth of February.

Divisible by four, except centuries, except every fourth century. The rule
is written out rather than looked up because it is three comparisons and
every reader can check it.
